fixes.explanation: David, king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3), is the one. The tabernacle remained until the time of David (Acts 7:45). That's a long run for a tent. I've seen cookie sheets retire sooner.

Elijah was a prophet in Israel (1 Kings 18:22), and that's a big name to grab. But the verse says the tabernacle remained until the time of David. David is the one who found favor in the sight of God and asked to provide a dwelling place for Him (Acts 7:46). Easy to mix up when the names start flying.

Daniel was one of the young men taken to Babylon (Daniel 1:1, 6), so he's a good name, just not for this verse. Stephen says the tabernacle remained until the time of David (Acts 7:45). David was king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). Daniel's story comes from a different chapter of the book.

Solomon, David's son (2 Samuel 12:24) and Israel's king (1 Kings 1:39), is the builder. Stephen says it plainly: "But it was Solomon who built the house for Him." (Acts 7:47). David had the idea and Solomon did the lifting. That's like the friend who says "we should open a bakery" while somebody else gets flour all over the apron.

Hezekiah was a king of Judah (2 Kings 18:1), so he's a fair guess for a king. But Stephen says, "But it was Solomon who built the house for Him." (Acts 7:47). Solomon was David's son (2 Samuel 12:24). David asked, and Solomon built.

Nehemiah is a builder, but he's known for rebuilding Jerusalem's wall (Nehemiah 2:17). Stephen says the house for God was built by Solomon, David's son (Acts 7:47; 2 Samuel 12:24). David asked to provide the dwelling place, and Solomon did the building. Different job, different builder.

Other way around, friend. Stephen says, "…the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands." (Acts 7:48). Solomon built a house, and Stephen says that about houses made by human hands. That's the turn the whole talk takes.

That's it. Stephen says, "…the Most High does not dwell in houses made by human hands." (Acts 7:48). Stephen had just mentioned Solomon building the house (Acts 7:47), so that line is a sharp turn. I'd have needed a minute to take that one in, and I only have a mustache to hold my notes.

Yes, the Holy Spirit. Stephen says, "You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did." (Acts 7:51). He says they always do it, not just once. He puts the council right next to their fathers. That's a line nobody can nod along to.

Pharaoh was Egypt's king (Exodus 5:1), and he does show up in Stephen's history (Acts 7:10). But in this line the one being resisted is the Holy Spirit. Stephen says, "You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did." (Acts 7:51).
True. Stephen says, "They even killed those who foretold the coming of the Righteous One." (Acts 7:52). He says it about the council's fathers. That's a heavy line, and the room is hearing it live.

No, and that's the opposite of what Stephen says. The words are, "…you are His betrayers and murderers…" (Acts 7:52). Students and followers would have been a much friendlier line. I think Stephen wasn't going for friendly.

Abraham is the man God told to leave his country, and he opens Stephen's history (Acts 7:2-3). But he isn't the one Stephen sees here. Stephen sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55).

Not at all, friend. Stephen says he sees heaven open, and the council "…covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him." (Acts 7:57). So calm left the building and listening went with it. I think they didn't want one more word.

False, and not even close. When Stephen says he sees heaven open, the council "…covered their ears, cried out in a loud voice, and rushed together at him." (Acts 7:57). Hands over ears is about as far from listening closely as you can get.
The verse doesn't say body. Stephen says, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." (Acts 7:59). This is a heavy moment. He asked Jesus to receive his spirit.
True. Acts 8:1 says, "And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen’s death." He's the young man whose feet the witnesses laid their garments at (Acts 7:58). He's right there when it happens.

Yes. "God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him." (Acts 8:2). It comes right after Saul's approval of Stephen's death (Acts 8:1). They didn't just bury him, they mourned deeply. I think that tells you how much he mattered to them.
The text doesn't name the council members here. It says God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him (Acts 8:2). The council had just been enraged and stoned him.

Yes. "Going from house to house, he dragged off men and women and put them in prison." (Acts 8:3). That's Saul, and he's going door to door. He did it to men and women both. It's a heavy way to close out the passage, and the text just says it plainly.
